originalGroup.material:
Learning what to ask

During my first week helping in a restaurant kitchen, I prepared a vegetable soup for the head cook to taste. She took a spoonful, closed her eyes and said ____1____. I assumed that silence meant failure.

I reached for the salt. She stopped my hand. "Why are you adding that?"

"You didn't say it was good."

"I was still ____2____," she replied.

I had expected an immediate judgment. Instead, she asked what I wanted to know. "Whether it tastes right," I said.

She suggested a more ____3____ question. I tasted again. The vegetables were tender, but I could barely notice the herbs. "Is the flavour too ____4____?"

Now we had something to discuss. She asked me to compare a spoonful from the pot with one containing a small extra pinch of herbs. I could hear her opinion later; first I needed to ____5____ the difference myself.

The second sample had more flavour, but I did not pour extra herbs straight into the whole pot. I checked the ____6____, then made a small adjustment. A useful trial was not permission to abandon careful measuring.

At lunch, a customer asked for the recipe. I felt ____7____, but the cook reminded me that one response could not settle everyone's taste. The next day, I might need to make the soup ____8____ for a different menu.

By the week's end, I had learned to bring questions as well as dishes. I stopped interpreting every ____9____ as disapproval and every compliment as a final ____10____. Feedback became more useful when I could explain what I was ____11____ to achieve.

The cook still corrected me, sometimes firmly. Yet I no longer felt that asking for detail showed ____12____. It showed I was willing to learn. I began to ____13____ my own work before waiting for someone else's verdict. The biggest change was not a new ingredient. It was a more ____14____ conversation, one that helped me decide what to try ____15____.

After the debate

Our debate team proposed opening the school library every weekend. We collected stories from students who lacked a quiet place to study and expected an easy victory. The benefits seemed ____1____.

Then the opposing team asked who would supervise the room. We had assumed existing staff could simply work more hours. Their questions exposed a ____2____ in our plan, and I felt myself becoming defensive.

During the break, I wanted a sharper reply. Our captain asked for a ____3____ instead. Could we identify what the other team had actually challenged?

"They don't care about students," I said.

"They asked about staff," she replied. "That isn't the ____4____ thing."

We returned to our notes. The need for study space remained ____5____, but our method depended on work nobody had agreed to provide. Repeating the need would not ____6____ that problem.

We lost the debate. Afterwards, I expected the captain to put our papers away. Instead, she invited the opposing team to help ____7____ a smaller proposal: one Saturday morning each month, with supervision arranged in advance.

Their speaker agreed. I was ____8____ by how readily we could cooperate after arguing. She said she had wanted the library open too, but could not support our unexplained staffing assumption.

The revised plan was not immediately accepted. We still had to discuss costs and responsibilities. Yet it gave the school a more ____9____ request than our first speech had offered.

I had treated criticism as an attempt to ____10____ our goal. Now I could see that some objections identified the conditions needed to make it ____11____. Changing the proposal did not mean pretending the original had been perfect, or that losing felt pleasant. It meant taking the strongest question ____12____.

The debate ended with a score. The work did not. We kept the first notes beside the revised plan as a ____13____ of how our thinking had changed. I still wanted to defend worthwhile ideas. I also wanted to become ____14____ at recognising when an opponent's question could help us ____15____ one.

"They don't care about students," I said.

"They asked about staff," she replied. "That isn't the ____4____ thing."

We returned to our notes. The need for study space remained ____5____, but our method depended on work nobody had agreed to provide. Repeating the need would not ____6____ that problem.
